newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav steelmakers seek more government help.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav steelmakers seek more government help.

text.p: Yugoslav steel producers sought stricter import controls from the Ministry of Economy on Tuesday to overcome unfair competition by Eastern European suppliers, an industry official said.
This was the second such plea adressed to the government in less than three months, head of the Yugoslav Association of Ferrous Metallurgy Arsenije Jovanovic told Reuters.
He said unfair competition from Eastern European suppliers who deliver goods at below-cost price levels threatened the industry.
"We call neither for a closed market nor for protective measures, but we want to eliminate all the factors disrupting fair competition," Jovanovic said.
Yugoslav steelworks are expected to produce a total of 650,000 tonnes of steel in 1996. The domestic market's needs are estimated at 500,000 tonnes.
He insisted Yugoslavia only needed to import 120,000 tonnes of steel products at the most -- far less than the 145,000 tonnes already imported in the first eight months of 1996.
"Importing more steel threatens the local industry's ability to recover from crippling sanctions," he said.
According to statistics, around 40 percent of imported products directly compete with localy produced equivalents.

"Almost 14 percent of the total Yugoslav ferrous metallurgy imports enters the country at prices lower than those on Western markets, and most of the unfair competition comes from the neighbouring Bulgaria and Romania," Jovanovic said.
While Jovanovic blamed suppliers for some problems, he also accused importers of manipulating import quotas for profit.
The association demanded the government introduce a system of tendering for quotas to reduce manipulation.
"At the moment quotas are reserved for the privileged, because they are never granted through tenders," he said.
The Ministry of Economy accepted the need for narrowing space for speculation among the importers.
Jovanovic argued the government should also impose stricter import controls, tightly police all regulations and abandon the law which freed many imports from taxation during sanctions.
"Sanctions have been suspended and will probably soon be lifted, making no further need for such a regulation," he said.
The Association for Ferrous Metallurgy, closely working with consultants from British Steel Plc, will soon outline its development plans for the next year.
The British experts, hired to help Yugoslav steel industry recover, will send their ideas by the end of September.

Their report should include recommendations about how the government should deal with this sector in the next two or three years of transition, Jovanovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
